opus-5.5.text:
Ramanujan is such a beautiful example to think about, because he's almost the extreme case of intuition outrunning proof. He'd write down these astonishing identities, infinite series for 1/π, partition congruences, mock theta functions, often with no proof at all, and many of them turned out to be true. Some took decades for other mathematicians to prove. A few were wrong. So he really shows you both sides: intuition is incredibly powerful, but on its own it isn't enough to tell you which of your beautiful ideas is actually correct.

That's exactly where I think AI for proving mathematics becomes valuable. Today's large language models are, in a sense, a bit like a very noisy Ramanujan. They can produce plausible-looking conjectures and arguments at enormous scale, but they also hallucinate. They'll confidently write a proof with a subtle gap, and if you're a human reading it, checking it can take as long as writing it yourself. So the bottleneck isn't really generating ideas anymore. It's verification.

What formal proof systems like Lean give you is a ground truth. When a proof compiles, it's correct, full stop. That changes the picture in two ways. First, it makes AI-generated mathematics trustworthy, so you don't need Hardy sitting next to Ramanujan for years sorting the gems from the mistakes. Second, and this is the part I find most exciting, verification gives you a perfect reward signal for training. The model can try millions of approaches, get unambiguous feedback on which ones work, and actually improve its reasoning instead of just its fluency. You're kind of building the intuition and the rigor together in a loop.

So I don't see it as AI replacing the Ramanujan-style genius. I see it as giving that kind of intuition a partner. Imagine a mathematician with a wild hunch who can hand it to a system that either proves it, finds a counterexample, or tells them precisely where the argument breaks. Hardy famously said that discovering Ramanujan was the one romantic incident in his life. I'd love a world where every curious student who has a Ramanujan-like spark has something like a Hardy available to them, one that is tireless, rigorous, and never gets bored checking the details.

And longer term, I think this matters well beyond pure math. Formal verification is how you get reasoning you can actually trust, whether it's in software, chip design, or science more broadly. Math just happens to be the cleanest place to start, because truth there is so well defined.

r002.rationale: The response describes proof feedback as improving AI reasoning and pairing rigor with intuition, but does not say that proving intuition-suggested results generates new mathematical intuitions.

fable-5.1.text:
Ramanujan is actually the example I come back to most often, because he's the strongest possible counterargument to the idea that mathematics is just formal manipulation. He was producing identities that nobody could derive, that he himself often couldn't prove, and a surprising fraction of them turned out to be correct. He said they came to him from a goddess in his dreams. Whatever you believe about that, the phenomenon is real: a human mind generating true, deep, non-obvious statements without going through the steps.

So when people ask me why we train AI to prove theorems, I think they often have Ramanujan in mind and they're asking, isn't the proving the boring part? Isn't the intuition the magic?

My view is that intuition and proof are not opposites. They're two halves of a loop. Ramanujan had Hardy. Hardy's job, for years, was to sit across from this torrent of conjectures and figure out which ones were actually true, which ones were true but already known, and which ones were subtly wrong. Some were wrong. Ramanujan's intuition was extraordinary, but it wasn't infallible, and without rigorous verification his notebooks would be a collection of beautiful guesses rather than a body of mathematics.

Now imagine Hardy could check a thousand conjectures a day instead of one a month. That's what formal verification gives you. A system like Lean doesn't care how elegant your idea is. It only cares whether each step follows. And once you can check at that scale, intuition becomes much more valuable, not less, because every wild guess can be tested instead of sitting in a drawer for eighty years.

That's really why I care about training models to prove rather than just to conjecture. If a model only produces plausible statements, you've built a very expensive Ramanujan with no Hardy. The failure mode is confident nonsense. A model that can also close the gap, write the proof and get it checked, is one you can actually trust, and trust is the whole point. A conjecture you can't verify is a mood. A proof is knowledge.

And there's something I find exciting about the reverse direction too. Once a system has proved thousands of things formally, you start to see what intuition even is. Ramanujan's gift probably came from pattern recognition over an enormous amount of mental computation with modular forms and partitions. These models are doing something structurally similar, just with far more examples and much faster feedback. So I don't think we're replacing the Ramanujan part. I think, for the first time, we might get to study it, and build something that does both sides of the table at once.

r001.rationale: The response says rigorous verification turns Ramanujan’s conjectures into a body of mathematics and that checking them at scale makes his intuition more valuable.

r002.rationale: The response says formal proofs can help study intuition and build a system that does both, but it does not clearly state that proving intuition-suggested results generates new mathematical intuitions.

astra-6.text:
I think Ramanujan’s intuition highlights why proving mathematics is such an interesting challenge for AI. There’s a difference between sensing that something is true and being able to explain, step by step, why it must be true. Mathematical discovery needs both.

If we train AI to prove theorems, we’re giving it a way to check ideas against a very demanding standard. A beautiful conjecture can be wrong, and an argument that sounds convincing can have a gap. Proof gives us a way to distinguish those cases.

But I wouldn’t equate proving theorems with the whole of mathematical creativity. There’s also choosing the right question, noticing an unexpected connection, or finding a definition that makes something suddenly clear. Ramanujan’s example invites us to ask whether AI can help with those parts, too.

What excites me is the possibility of a partnership: a mathematician has an intuition, and an AI helps explore its consequences and work toward a proof. That could let people pursue ideas that would otherwise be too difficult or time-consuming to develop.

r002.rationale: It describes AI helping explore an intuition’s consequences and work toward a proof, but does not state that proving intuition-suggested results can generate new mathematical intuitions.

sol-6.1.text:
Ramanujan is a wonderful example of how mathematical discovery can run ahead of our ability to explain it. He could see patterns and formulate extraordinary conjectures, but establishing why those conjectures were true was often a separate, substantial task.

I see training AI to prove mathematics as a way to bring those two activities closer together. You want a system that can propose something surprising, but also work through the reasoning and check whether it holds. Formal proof gives you a precise way to distinguish a beautiful idea from a correct one.

And proving things can itself lead to new intuition. When you understand why a result is true, you start seeing connections and asking better questions. So the exciting possibility is that AI could help mathematicians explore more ideas and turn some of those ideas into reliable knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response says proving Ramanujan’s conjectures was a separate task, but does not state that learning to write proofs amplified the impact of his mathematics.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says proving things can lead to new intuition, connections, and better questions.
